proof_skeleton_nl: Normalize the original summand using the elementary identity ((q^d;q^d)_k)^2/(q^{2d};q^{2d})_k=(q^d;q^d)_k/(-q^d;q^d)_k, and call the resulting normalized sum S(q). Multiply by the explicit clearing factor D_{d,n}(q)=∏_{s=0}^{n-1}(-q^d;q^d)_s to form H(q)=D(q)S(q). The first substantive input is the strictly weaker lemma that H(q) is a Laurent polynomial divisible by [n]_q; write H(q)=[n]_q J(q). Independently, factor the claimed right-hand side as [n]_q G_{r,n}(q) q^{r(1-n)/2}. The bottleneck lemma then compares the quotient J(q) with D(q)G_{r,n}(q)q^{r(1-n)/2} at every primitive nth root of unity, including first derivative. The abstract double-root criterion upgrades this comparison to Φ_n(q)^2-divisibility of the quotient difference. Multiplying back by [n]_q yields divisibility of D(q)(S(q)-R(q)) by [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2 in the Laurent polynomial ring. Finally, use the coprimality of D(q) with the modulus and the abstract localization-cancellation lemma to cancel D(q) from the congruence, and then replace S(q) by the original sum T(q) via the initial normalization identity. This avoids the previously falsified auxiliary-parameter branch and keeps all hard content isolated in the explicit primitive-root quotient-comparison bottleneck.

steps.derives: From the theorem hypotheses n > 1 and n ≡ 1 mod 2d, conclude that n is odd and gcd(d,n)=1.
steps.trivial_justification: Write n = 1 + 2dt for some integer t. Then n is odd. If a positive integer c divides both d and n, then c also divides n - 2dt = 1, so c = 1. Therefore gcd(d,n)=1.

steps.derives: Define T(q) = ∑_{k=0}^{n-1} [3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k (q^d;q^d)_k^2 q^{k(d-dk-2r)/2} / (q^{2d};q^{2d})_k, define S(q) = ∑_{k=0}^{n-1} [3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k (q^d;q^d)_k q^{k(d-dk-2r)/2} / (-q^d;q^d)_k, define R(q) = [rn]_q q^{r(1-n)/2}, define D(q) = ∏_{s=0}^{n-1} (-q^d;q^d)_s, define H(q) = D(q)S(q), define G(q) = ∑_{j=0}^{r-1} q^{jn}, and define M(q) = [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2.
steps.trivial_justification: This step only introduces abbreviations for the original sum, the normalized sum, the right-hand side, the clearing factor, the cleared sum, the geometric quotient, and the target modulus.

steps.derives: T(q) = S(q).
steps.trivial_justification: Lemma L1 rewrites the factor ((q^d;q^d)_k)^2/(q^{2d};q^{2d})_k in each summand of T(q) as (q^d;q^d)_k/(-q^d;q^d)_k. After this termwise replacement, the resulting finite sum is exactly the definition of S(q).

steps.derives: There exists a Laurent polynomial J(q) in Z[q^{±1}] such that H(q) = [n]_q J(q).
steps.trivial_justification: Lemma L3 states that H(q) lies in Z[q^{±1}] and is divisible by [n]_q in that ring. By the definition of divisibility, a quotient J(q) exists with H(q) = [n]_q J(q).

steps.derives: R(q) = [n]_q G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2}, and therefore D(q)R(q) = [n]_q D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2}.
steps.trivial_justification: Lemma L4 gives [rn]_q = [n]_q G(q). Substituting this identity into the definition R(q) = [rn]_q q^{r(1-n)/2} yields the first formula. Multiplying by D(q) gives the second formula.

From A1, H(q)=D(q)S(q). Hence D(q)(S(q)-R(q)) = H(q) - D(q)R(q). By A3, H(q) = [n]_q J(q). By A4, D(q)R(q) = [n]_q D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2}. Substituting these two identities into H(q)-D(q)R(q) gives [n]_q J(q) - [n]_q D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2}, and factoring out [n]_q yields the displayed identity.

steps.derives: If B(q) = D(q) q^{r(1-n)/2} G(q), then for every primitive nth root of unity ζ one has J(ζ) = B(ζ) and J'(ζ) = B'(ζ).
steps.trivial_justification: Step A3 provides exactly the hypothesis H(q) = [n]_q J(q) required by Lemma L6, and the definitions of D(q), H(q), and G(q) from A1 match the objects in that lemma. Therefore Lemma L6 gives the stated equalities of values and derivatives at primitive nth roots.

steps.derives: Φ_n(q)^2 divides J(q) - D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2} in Z[q^{±1}].
steps.trivial_justification: Apply Lemma L5 with A(q)=J(q) and B(q)=D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2}. Step A6 supplies the hypotheses that these two Laurent polynomials have equal values and equal first q-derivatives at every primitive nth root of unity.

steps.derives: M(q) divides [n]_q ( J(q) - D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2} ) in Z[q^{±1}].
steps.trivial_justification: By A7, there exists a Laurent polynomial U(q) such that J(q) - D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2} = Φ_n(q)^2 U(q). Multiplying by [n]_q and using the definition M(q) = [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2 from A1 gives [n]_q ( J(q) - D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2} ) = M(q)U(q). Hence M(q) divides the displayed Laurent polynomial.

steps.derives: M(q) divides D(q)(S(q)-R(q)) in Z[q^{±1}].
steps.trivial_justification: Step A5 identifies D(q)(S(q)-R(q)) exactly with [n]_q ( J(q) - D(q)G(q) q^{r(1-n)/2} ). Step A8 says that M(q) divides this latter Laurent polynomial. Replacing the right-hand side in A5 by the equal expression therefore shows that M(q) divides D(q)(S(q)-R(q)).

steps.derives: The polynomial M(q) has constant term 1; in particular q is coprime to M(q).
steps.trivial_justification: By A1, M(q) = [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2. Since n>1, the polynomial [n]_q = 1+q+⋯+q^{n-1} has constant term 1, and the cyclotomic polynomial Φ_n(q) also has constant term 1. Therefore M(q) has constant term 1. A polynomial with constant term 1 is not divisible by q, so q and M(q) are coprime.

steps.derives: D(q)S(q) ≡ D(q)R(q) mod M(q).
steps.trivial_justification: Step A9 gives a Laurent polynomial U(q) with D(q)(S(q)-R(q)) = M(q)U(q). Any Laurent polynomial can be written as q^{-e}P(q) for some integer e ≥ 0 and some polynomial P(q). By A10, q is coprime to M(q), so the denominator q^e of U(q) is coprime to M(q). Therefore U(q) is an admissible witness in the localized congruence definition, and the displayed identity is exactly the statement D(q)S(q) ≡ D(q)R(q) mod M(q).

steps.derives: H(q) is a Laurent polynomial in Z[q^{±1}].
steps.trivial_justification: Step A3 gives H(q) = [n]_q J(q) with J(q) Laurent and [n]_q polynomial. Therefore H(q) is Laurent.

steps.derives: The rational function S(q) has a denominator of the form q^e D(q) for some integer e ≥ 0.
steps.trivial_justification: By A12, write H(q) = q^{-e}P(q) for some integer e ≥ 0 and some polynomial P(q). Since A1 defines H(q)=D(q)S(q), rearranging gives S(q)=P(q)/(q^e D(q)). Thus S(q) has a denominator of the form q^e D(q).

steps.derives: gcd(D(q), M(q)) = 1 in Z[q].
steps.trivial_justification: Step A0 gives that n is odd and gcd(d,n)=1. Applying Lemma L2 to d and n yields gcd(D(q), [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2)=1. By the definition of M(q) in A1, this is exactly gcd(D(q), M(q))=1.

steps.derives: The rational function S(q) has a denominator coprime to M(q).
steps.trivial_justification: By A13, S(q) has a denominator q^e D(q) for some e ≥ 0. Step A10 shows q is coprime to M(q), so q^e is coprime to M(q). Step A14 shows D(q) is coprime to M(q). Therefore the product q^e D(q) is coprime to M(q), giving a denominator of S(q) that is coprime to M(q).

steps.derives: The rational function R(q) has a denominator coprime to M(q).
steps.trivial_justification: Since n is odd by A0, the exponent r(1-n)/2 is an integer. Therefore R(q) = [rn]_q q^{r(1-n)/2} is a Laurent polynomial whose denominator is a power of q. By A10, q is coprime to M(q), so every power of q is also coprime to M(q). Hence R(q) has a denominator coprime to M(q).

steps.derives: S(q) ≡ R(q) mod M(q).
steps.trivial_justification: Apply Lemma L7 with F(q)=S(q), G(q)=R(q), D(q)=D_{d,n}(q), and M(q)=M(q). Step A10 supplies M(0)=1. Step A14 supplies gcd(D(q),M(q))=1. Steps A15 and A16 show that S(q) and R(q) have denominators coprime to M(q). Step A11 gives D(q)S(q) ≡ D(q)R(q) mod M(q). Lemma L7 therefore yields S(q) ≡ R(q) mod M(q).

steps.derives: T(q) ≡ R(q) mod M(q).
steps.trivial_justification: Step A2 identifies T(q) with S(q). Replacing S(q) by T(q) in the congruence from A17 gives T(q) ≡ R(q) mod M(q).

steps.derives: Let [m]_q = (1−q^m)/(1−q), let (a;q)_k = ∏_{j=0}^{k−1} (1−aq^j), let (a,b,c;q)_k = (a;q)_k (b;q)_k (c;q)_k, and let Φ_n(q) be the nth cyclotomic polynomial. Prove that for positive integers d and r with gcd(d,r)=1 and r ≤ d, and for every integer n > 1 with n ≡ 1 mod 2d, we have ∑_{k=0}^{n−1} [3dk+r]_q (q^r,q^r,q^d;q^{2d})_k (q^d;q^d)_k^2 q^(k(d−dk−2r)/2) / (q^{2d};q^{2d})_k ≡ [rn]_q q^(r(1−n)/2) mod [n]_q Φ_n(q)^2.
steps.trivial_justification: Step A18 is the congruence T(q) ≡ R(q) mod M(q). Unfolding the abbreviations T(q), R(q), and M(q) introduced in A1 produces exactly the root theorem statement.
